summary: Lists the possible values for IPv4 subnets. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1878.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1860 is a lookup table for IPv4 subnet masks. It shows each mask in several forms and gives examples of how a block can be divided into subnets and hosts.

how does cidr notation match a subnet mask
subtitle: A reference table of IPv4 subnet masks and the address blocks they describe.

tldr.problem: Readers needed a reference for IPv4 subnet mask values in several notations and for the address counts associated with each mask.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists masks from /1 through /32 with hexadecimal, CIDR, and decimal forms, classful equivalents, and address counts, plus examples for two block sizes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1860 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1878.

today: RFC 1860 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1878.

sections.title: What the Table Contains
sections.content:
The memo itemizes potential values for IPv4 subnets. For each listed mask it gives hexadecimal and decimal forms, CIDR notation, a classful equivalent where shown, and the number of addresses in the block.

The mask list runs from /1 to /32. The memo is a reference table; it does not define a protocol for allocating or routing those blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: The table lets readers look up an IPv4 mask in different notations. It also shows the size of the address block represented by each mask.

sections.title: Mask Notations and Address Counts
sections.content:
Each table row pairs a mask's hexadecimal value with CIDR notation and a dotted-decimal value. The table also gives an approximate number of addresses using K and M units, and lists a Class A, B, or C equivalent for some masks. For example, the row for /24 lists 255.255.255.0 and 256 addresses.

The last rows mark /31 as unusable and describe /32 as a single host route. The RFC does not provide a classful equivalent for every row.
sections.plainLanguage: Find a mask's row to see its CIDR and dotted-decimal forms and the block size. The table also marks /31 as unusable and /32 as a single host route.

sections.title: Examples of Subnetting Blocks
sections.content:
The RFC gives example tables for starting blocks of /16 and /24. Each example shows how many bits are used to divide the block, the resulting mask, the effective number of subnets, and the effective hosts per subnet.

The examples exclude subnet addresses with all zeroes or all ones, and also exclude host addresses with all zeroes or all ones. The counts in the examples follow those exclusions.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how changing the mask divides a starting block into more or fewer subnets. Their counts leave out subnet and host values that are all zeroes or all ones.

references.text: Fuller, V., Li, T., Yu, J., and K. Varadhan, "Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR): an Address Assignment and Aggregation Strategy", RFC 1519, September 1993.
